Under section 3(1) of the Contributory Negligence and Personal Injuries Act 1953, if the accident was caused partly by your fault and partly by another person’s fault, your claim is **not defeated** merely because you contributed to it [CITE:1]. Instead, the court reduces the damages recoverable to the extent it considers just and equitable, having regard to your share of responsibility for the damage [CITE:1].

For this Act, “fault” includes negligence, breach of a statutory duty, and other acts or omissions giving rise to liability in tort or to the defence of contributory negligence [CITE:3]. Contributory negligence focuses on whether you failed to take reasonable care of your own safety in the circumstances and were blameworthy to the extent that you contributed to your own injury [CITE:14]. The other party need not show that you breached a duty of care owed to someone else, but must show that you owed yourself a duty to take care of your own safety [CITE:2].

The test asks whether you ought objectively to have foreseen that failing to act prudently could injure you and failed to take reasonable measures against that foreseeable harm [CITE:14]. The expected standard is that of a person of ordinary prudence [CITE:2].

If contributory negligence is established, the court apportions responsibility by considering the relative causative importance of each party’s conduct and their relative moral blameworthiness; this is a broad, fact-sensitive assessment rather than a purely mathematical calculation [CITE:13][CITE:11]. The court must record the total damages that would have been recoverable without your contributory negligence and then apply the appropriate reduction [CITE:1].

For illustration, if the court assessed total damages at $100,000 and attributed 20% of the responsibility to you, the recoverable damages would be $80,000 [CITE:1].

Where multiple people caused indivisible injury, you may recover the full amount remaining after any contributory-negligence reduction from any one of them whose conduct caused the injury; allocation between those defendants is a separate contribution issue [CITE:12][CITE:18]. In short, your own blame ordinarily **reduces rather than extinguishes** your damages [CITE:1][CITE:10]

As at 2026-11-06, for an action for damages arising from negligence or breach of duty, the limitation period generally depends on whether the claim includes personal injuries and when you first acquired the legally required knowledge. [CITE:1][CITE:2]

### If your claim includes personal injuries

Section 24A(2) applies where the damages claimed consist of or include personal injuries to you or another person. [CITE:1]

The section 24A deadline is the later of: [CITE:1]

- Three years from the date the cause of action accrued; and
- Three years from the earliest date on which you had the knowledge required to bring the action.

For negligence requiring proof of damage, the cause of action is generally complete only when duty, breach and damage have all been established. [CITE:15]

### If the claim is for other damage

For an action not covered by the personal-injury rule, section 24A(3) provides a deadline based on the later of: [CITE:1]

- Six years from the date the cause of action accrued; and
- Three years from the earliest date on which you had both the required knowledge and a right to bring the action.

### What “knowledge” means

Knowing only that you were injured is generally insufficient. The statutory knowledge requirements include: [CITE:1]

- Knowledge that the injury or damage was attributable to the alleged careless act or omission;
- Knowledge of the defendant’s identity;
- If another person is alleged to have committed the act or omission, knowledge of that person’s identity and the additional facts needed to bring proceedings against the defendant; and
- Knowledge of material facts showing that the injury or damage was sufficiently serious to justify proceedings against a defendant who did not dispute liability and could satisfy a judgment.

You do not need to know that the conduct legally amounts to negligence, nuisance or breach of duty; that legal conclusion is irrelevant for determining the knowledge date. [CITE:1]

Accordingly, if you first learned all the legally relevant facts much later, that later date may move the section 24A deadline, subject to the following cap. [CITE:1]

### The final 15-year cap

Section 24B imposes an overriding 15-year limit on actions for negligence, nuisance or breach of duty covered by section 24A. [CITE:2][CITE:9]

The “starting date” is the date of the alleged negligent or breach-of-duty act or omission to which the injury or damage is attributable; where there is more than one such act or omission, the starting date is the last of those dates. [CITE:2]

The claim is barred after 15 years from that starting date even if the cause of action had not yet accrued by then. [CITE:2][CITE:9] Later discovery of the injury or the wrong therefore cannot extend the claim beyond this final backstop. [CITE:9]

Different negligent failures may constitute different causes of action; the relevant question is whether there was in substance one or multiple breaches of duty by the same defendant, rather than how many separate components make up the claimed damage. [CITE:10]

The exact deadline cannot be calculated without the date the injury or damage occurred, the date you first met the knowledge requirements, whether there were several alleged careless acts or omissions, and whether the claim includes personal injuries. [CITE:1][CITE:2][CITE:4] If the defendant raises limitation as a defence in its pleadings, the claimant bears the burden of showing that the claim falls within the applicable limitation period. [CITE:13]

As at 2026-11-06, where an action is based on fraud, or the fraud concealed the right of action, the general limitation clock does not start until you actually discovered the fraud or could, with reasonable diligence, have discovered it. [CITE:1] In practical terms, the clock generally starts on the earlier of actual discovery and the date when reasonable inquiries would have revealed the fraud. [CITE:1] Section 29 applies the same postponement rule where the claim seeks relief from the consequences of a mistake. [CITE:1]

The applicable time limit then depends on the type of claim:

- **Contract or tort:** The general period is six years from when the cause of action accrued, subject to the Limitation Act. [CITE:5]
- **Negligence, nuisance or breach-of-duty damages:** For damage other than personal injury, the period is six years from accrual or three years from when you first had both the necessary knowledge and the right to sue, if the three-year period ends later. [CITE:4] Knowledge includes what you could reasonably have been expected to acquire from observable or ascertainable facts, although you need not know every detail of what went wrong. [CITE:3] An overriding 15-year period runs from the relevant negligent act or omission. [CITE:19]
- **Fraud or fraudulent breach of trust by a trustee:** A beneficiary has no prescribed limitation period for specified fraud-related trust claims, including recovery of trust property or proceeds held or converted by the trustee. [CITE:2]
- **Consumer unfair practices:** An action under section 6 must generally be commenced within two years after the later of the last material event or the consumer’s knowledge of the unfair practice; reasonable ascertainability and appropriate expert advice are taken into account. [CITE:8]

Therefore, for an ordinary concealed-fraud claim, the starting point is actual discovery or the earlier date on which reasonable diligence would have discovered the fraud. [CITE:1]

As at 2026-11-06, section 7 of the Defamation Act 1957 provides an **“offer of amends”** procedure that can prevent libel or slander proceedings where words were published innocently in relation to the person aggrieved. [CITE:1]

### Effect of an offer of amends

- A publisher who claims that the words were published **innocently** may make an offer of amends. [CITE:1]
- If the person aggrieved accepts the offer and it is **duly performed**, proceedings for libel or slander cannot be taken or continued against the person making the offer concerning that publication, although this does not prejudice proceedings against any other person jointly responsible for it. [CITE:1]
- If the offer is not accepted, it may still provide a defence in proceedings if the statutory requirements are proved: the publication was made by the defendant or innocently in relation to the claimant, the offer was made as soon as practicable after the defendant received notice that the words were or might be defamatory, and the offer has not been withdrawn. [CITE:1]

### What “innocently” means

The first limb of the statutory test applies where the publisher did not intend the words to be of or concerning that person and did not know of circumstances by virtue of which they might be understood to refer to that person. [CITE:2]

The alternative limb applies where the words were not defamatory on their face and the publisher did not know of circumstances by virtue of which they might be understood to be defamatory of that person. [CITE:2]

In either case, the publisher must have exercised **all reasonable care** concerning the publication; merely not intending to refer to the person is therefore not necessarily sufficient. [CITE:2]

### Form of the offer

The offer must be expressed to be made for the purposes of section 7 and must be accompanied by an affidavit specifying the facts relied upon to show that the publication was innocent. [CITE:1]

For purposes of the statutory defence, the publisher may introduce evidence only of the facts specified in that affidavit to prove that the publication was innocent. [CITE:1]

An offer of amends ordinarily means publishing or joining in the publication of a suitable correction and a sufficient apology. If copies containing the words were distributed by or with the publisher’s knowledge, it also means taking reasonably practicable steps to notify recipients that the words are alleged to be defamatory. [CITE:1]

If the publisher was not the author of the words, the defence under section 7(1)(b) is unavailable unless the publisher proves that the author wrote them without malice. [CITE:2]

### Criminal-law distinction

Section 7 concerns proceedings for libel or slander. [CITE:1] The supplied Penal Code provisions separately define defamation and create an offence for printing or engraving matter known, or having good reason to believe, to be defamatory; the supplied provisions do not state that an offer of amends under section 7 prevents a prosecution under those provisions. [CITE:3] [CITE:10]

As at 2026-11-06, on the supplied consolidated Penal Code, hurting someone is not automatically an offence if the force is exercised in the statutory right of private defence: nothing done in the exercise of that right is an offence. [CITE:7]

The following conditions apply:

- Every person may defend their own body, and the body of another person, against an offence affecting the human body, subject to statutory restrictions. [CITE:5]
- The right begins when the defender **reasonably believes** that there is danger to the body arising from an offence, attempt, or threat, even if the offence has not yet occurred. [CITE:2]
- The right continues only while that reasonable belief of danger continues. [CITE:2]
- The force used must not inflict more harm than is reasonably necessary in the circumstances. [CITE:4]
- There is no right of private defence where there is a reasonable opportunity to obtain protection from a public authority, such as the police. [CITE:4]
- For certain assaults, the right extends to causing death where, for example, the defender reasonably believes that death or grievous hurt will otherwise result. [CITE:1] For other offences, the right extends only to causing harm other than death. [CITE:10]

If the requirements for private defence are not met, deliberately or knowingly causing bodily pain, disease, infirmity, or unconsciousness may constitute voluntarily causing hurt. [CITE:20] Where the offender did not intend or know that grievous hurt was likely but actually caused it, section 323A provides for imprisonment of up to five years, a fine of up to $10,000, or both. As at 2026-11-06, on the consolidated text of the Evidence Act 1893 in force from 9 March 2025 supplied in the sources, the party must first prove the **loss (or destruction, or unavailability) of the original document**, because that fact opens the only gateway to secondary evidence of its contents. [CITE:1][CITE:7]

## 1. The starting rule: primary evidence is the default

Documents must generally be proved by primary evidence, which means the document itself produced for the court's inspection, except in the cases mentioned in section 67. [CITE:4][CITE:13] The contents of a document may otherwise be proved by primary or by secondary evidence. [CITE:9] Section 67(1)(c) is the relevant gateway: secondary evidence of the existence, condition or contents of a document may be given where the original "has been destroyed or lost", or where the party offering evidence of its contents cannot, for any reason not arising from their own default or neglect, produce it in reasonable time. [CITE:7]

Accordingly, the fact that must be established first is one of the section 67(1)(c) conditions — most commonly that the original has been lost or destroyed, and that the inability to produce it does not arise from the party's own default or neglect. [CITE:7]

## 2. Why the party bears that burden

Section 106 places the burden of proving any fact necessary to be proved so as to enable a person to give evidence of another fact on the person wishing to give that evidence, and its illustration (b) states this expressly for the lost-document situation: a person wishing to prove by secondary evidence the contents of a lost document must prove that the document has been lost. [CITE:1] Section 105 states the same general principle, namely that the burden of proof of a particular fact lies on the person who wishes the court to believe in its existence. [CITE:12] Proof of the loss is therefore the condition that unlocks admissibility, and it is not a matter the court raises on the party's behalf; a fact of which the court takes judicial notice need not be proved. [CITE:18]

## 3. The order in which proof must be given

Under section 138(2), where the proposed fact may be proved only upon proof of another fact, that other fact must be proved before the first is given, unless the party undertakes to give proof of it and the court is satisfied with the undertaking. [CITE:3] The illustration to section 138 uses the lost-document example directly: the fact that the original is lost must be proved by the person proposing to produce the copy before the copy is produced. [CITE:3] The court also has a discretion under section 138(3) to permit evidence of the contents to be given before the loss is proved, or to require the loss to be proved first. [CITE:3]

## 4. What may then be adduced as secondary evidence

Section 65 defines secondary evidence to include copies made from the original by technical processes that ensure the accuracy of the copy, copies compared with such copies, copies made from or compared with the original, counterparts against parties who did not execute them, and oral accounts of the contents given by someone who has personally seen the document. [CITE:5] A copy transcribed from a copy but afterwards compared with the original qualifies; the same copy without such comparison does not, and an oral account of a copy, photograph or machine-copy is not secondary evidence of the original. [CITE:5]

## 5. Two related points

As at 2026-11-06, yes. The principal statutory scheme is the Second Schedule of the Legal Profession Act 1966, which is given effect by section 75B and is headed "Redress for inadequate professional services" [CITE:2]. The consolidated text reproduced in the sources is stated to be in force from 17 April 2025, and each source notes that Singapore Statutes Online should be checked for the latest version [CITE:1].

**1. What the scheme covers**

Section 75B(1) applies the Second Schedule to services provided by solicitors on or after 1 September 1998 which are not of the quality that it is reasonable to expect of them [CITE:2]. Section 75B(2) and (2A) extend the Second Schedule, with any modifications prescribed by the Minister, to solicitors registered under section 36E who provide Singapore-law services in a Joint Law Venture, Qualifying Foreign Law Practice or licensed foreign law practice, and to foreign lawyers registered under section 36B who practise Singapore law [CITE:2].

**2. What the Council can do**

Where it appears to the Council that the professional services instructed by a client have not been of the quality reasonably expected of the solicitor, the Council may give directions concerning that solicitor [CITE:1]. One direction is a determination that the solicitor's costs are to be limited to a specified amount, together with directions to comply with the permitted requirements needed to give effect to that determination [CITE:1]. Another is a direction that the solicitor secure rectification at the solicitor's or the firm's expense [CITE:1]. The extract of paragraph 2(1)(b) in the sources is cut off mid-sentence, so the complete list of available directions cannot be set out from these sources [CITE:1].

**3. No court proceedings are required**

Nothing in the Second Schedule requires a client to commence civil proceedings before the Council acts [CITE:1]. The Council must not take directions unless it is satisfied that, in all the circumstances of the case, it is appropriate to do so [CITE:1]. In deciding that, the Council may have regard to any remedy reasonably expected to be available to the client in civil proceedings, to whether it is reasonable to expect the client to begin such proceedings where they have not, and to whether the solicitor responded to, or attempted to resolve, a matter where the client had tried to contact the solicitor [CITE:1].

**4. Time limit and effect on the bill**

The Council must not take directions on a complaint of conduct made to the Society after the expiry of three years from the date of the conduct [CITE:1]. Where the Council has directed that costs be limited to a specified amount, the amount charged in any bill is deemed to be limited to that amount for assessment purposes, and where the bill has not yet been assessed you are deemed liable to pay only that amount, despite any statutory provision or agreement to the contrary [CITE:11]. If the bill has already been assessed, the direction ceases to have effect so far as it relates to costs [CITE:11].

**5. Client fees and enforcement of a direction**

The Council may, by rules made with the concurrence of the Chief Justice, provide for payment of a prescribed fee by clients in respect of whom it is asked to consider taking steps, and any fee so paid must be repaid if the Council takes any of the steps [CITE:11]. The Council may also direct the solicitor to pay it the fee payable to the client and an amount calculated as the cost of dealing with the complaint, or a reasonable contribution towards that cost [CITE:11]. If a solicitor, law corporation or limited liability law partnership fails to comply with a direction, any person may make a complaint to a Judge about that failure, no other proceedings may be brought in respect of it, and the Judge may direct that the direction be treated, for enforcement, as if it were contained in an order of the General Division of the High Court [CITE:11].

**6. Other statutory routes that do not involve a damages claim**

- *Disciplinary complaint.* A complaint of the conduct of a regulated legal practitioner must be made to the Society in writing, must include a statement about any other complaint arising from the same facts, and must be supported by a statutory declaration unless made by a public officer or an officer of the Institute, and the Council must refer qualifying complaints to the Chairperson of the Inquiry Panel [CITE:8]. Where the six-year period has expired (or, for alleged fraud, the six years from the date the fraud could with reasonable diligence have been discovered, if that is later), the Council may, with the court's permission, refer the complaint or information to the Chairperson of the Inquiry Panel [CITE:5]. Permission is sought by originating application supported by an affidavit explaining the delay and why referral is justified, and the application must be served on the practitioner [CITE:5].
- *Foreign lawyers and law experts.* A complaint of conduct must be made in writing to the Registrar and, subject to exceptions, supported by a statutory declaration; the Registrar must then furnish a copy to the foreign lawyer or law expert and ask the Chief Justice to appoint a complaints committee [CITE:10]. A complaints committee may warn, reprimand, or order payment of a penalty of up to $20,000, and may make orders for costs [CITE:4].
- *Criminal proceedings.* Where an advocate appears for the defence, a court may disallow costs as between the advocate and the client where costs were incurred unreasonably or improperly, or were wasted by a failure to conduct the proceedings with reasonable competence and expedition, and the advocate must be given a reasonable opportunity to appear and show cause [CITE:7].
- *Fee agreements.* Questions concerning the validity or effect of an agreement of the kind covered by section 111 must be determined by the court on an originating application, and no action or suit may be brought on such an agreement; the court may enforce the agreement if it is fair and reasonable, or declare it void if it is unfair or unreasonable [CITE:6].

**7. How the scheme differs from a negligence claim**

In a professional negligence claim, the central question is whether the advice given or omitted fell below the standard of the reasonably competent lawyer, assessed by asking what such a lawyer in the same position would have advised in the circumstances at the time, and not with the benefit of hindsight, with a lawyer not liable merely because an error of judgment turned out to be wrong [CITE:12]. In the Sports Connection decision, the court held that advice which was illusory or fanciful was hardly advice falling within the duty of any reasonably competent lawyer [CITE:9]. The Second Schedule uses a different formulation, namely whether the services were of the quality reasonably expected of the solicitor, and it expressly directs the Council to weigh the availability and likely pursuit of civil remedies [CITE:1]. Proceedings against the Attorney-General, the Society, the Council and related bodies for acts done under the Act are barred unless the court is satisfied the act was done in bad faith or with malice [CITE:3].

**What the sources do not cover**

The sources do not set out the practical procedure for lodging and pursuing a Second Schedule complaint, the complete list of directions available, or the terms of the rules made under paragraph 11 of the Second Schedule, which the Act contemplates and which govern how the scheme operates in the foreign-law-practitioner cases [CITE:2]. The latest consolidated Second Schedule, the rules made under it, and the Law Society's practice guidance would need to be checked on Singapore Statutes Online.

As at 2026-11-06, **an ordinary civil claim generally does not die merely because the person who brought it dies**, although different types of proceedings have special rules. [CITE:1][CITE:2][CITE:14]

### Ordinary civil claims

- Section 10(1) of the Civil Law Act 1909 provides that, subject to the section, a cause of action vested in a deceased person survives for the benefit of their estate, while a cause of action against the deceased survives against their estate. [CITE:1]
- Section 10 itself governs survival of the cause of action but does not set out the complete procedural rules for substituting the estate or continuing an already-pending civil action. [CITE:1]
- One supplied High Court decision accepted that a claim could be pursued on a deceased person’s behalf where the person had died after commencement of the suit. [CITE:16]

There are important exceptions and limitations:

- Causes of action for defamation or seduction, for inducing a spouse to leave or remain apart, and for damages based on adultery do not survive under section 10. [CITE:1]
- A bereavement claim under section 21 does not survive for the benefit of the claimant’s estate. [CITE:5]
- Even where a civil cause of action survives, recoverable damages for the estate cannot include exemplary damages or loss of income relating to a period after death; special rules also apply where the death was caused by the act or omission giving rise to the claim. [CITE:1]

### Other proceedings

- **Arbitration:** An arbitration agreement is not discharged by a party’s death and remains enforceable by or against the deceased party’s personal representative; the arbitrator’s authority is also not revoked by that death. [CITE:3]
- **Criminal proceedings:** If the deceased person was the accused, every charge or criminal proceeding abates, and the court must order that it abates if satisfied the accused is dead. [CITE:2]
- **Criminal appeals:** A relevant appeal may be commenced or continued by a person approved by the General Division of the High Court. Approval is limited to specified categories, including a spouse, personal representative, or qualifying family or similarly connected person, and the application must be made within one year after death; without approval, a commenced appeal finally abates. [CITE:9]
- **Bankruptcy applications:** If a debtor dies after a bankruptcy application has been made, the proceedings ordinarily continue as if the debtor were alive unless the court directs otherwise. [CITE:11]
- **Government suits:** A Government suit against a deceased person, or a suit continuing after a defendant dies, does not abate; the personal representatives, next of kin, or an official administrator may intervene to defend it. [CITE:15]
- **Proceedings by or against an official:** Death, resignation, absence, or removal from office does not discontinue or abate such proceedings; they may be carried on by the person appointed to perform the office’s duties. [CITE:12]
- **Parliamentary election applications:** An application under section 90 abates upon the death of the sole claimant or the survivor of several claimants, although substitution of a claimant is available within one calendar month after publication of notice of abatement or such further time as the judge allows. [CITE:14]

**In short:** for an ordinary civil action, the underlying claim generally survives the claimant’s death; for a criminal charge against the deceased, the proceeding generally abates, subject to the special appeal procedure. [CITE:1][CITE:2][CITE:9]

As at 2026-11-06, a court should use a staged approach under section 9A of the Interpretation Act 1965 and the Court of Appeal’s three-step framework, rather than select a meaning from isolated words. [CITE:1] [CITE:13]

1. **Identify the possible interpretations.** The court first reads the provision’s text, considering its context within the written law as a whole. [CITE:13]

2. **Determine the purpose of the written law.** The court ordinarily gleans the purpose from the text itself; where the text and context do not sufficiently disclose the purpose, extrinsic material may assist. [CITE:4] [CITE:13]

3. **Apply the purposive preference.** Section 9A(1) requires the court to prefer an interpretation promoting the purpose or object underlying the written law, whether that purpose is expressly stated or not. [CITE:1]

4. **Consider extrinsic material only where section 9A permits it.** Material outside the written law may be considered to confirm the ordinary meaning of the provision, or where the provision is ambiguous or obscure, or where its ordinary meaning in context produces a manifestly absurd or unreasonable result. [CITE:1] Permitted material includes, among other things, explanatory statements, ministerial speeches, Parliamentary debate records, relevant treaties, and documents declared relevant by the written law. [CITE:1]

5. **Give primacy to the text and statutory context.** Extrinsic material may assist interpretation but must not be used to give a provision a meaning that contradicts its express text, except in very limited circumstances. [CITE:13]

6. **Compare and select.** The court compares the possible interpretations against the purpose of the statute and prefers the interpretation that furthers that purpose while remaining consistent with the provision’s text and statutory context. [CITE:13]

As at 2026-11-06, **yes**. Two separate statutory regimes apply: a death-specific preservation duty under the Coroners Act 2010, and a continuing record-keeping duty under the Healthcare Services Act 2020 that applies to healthcare service licensees, including hospitals. [CITE:1] [CITE:2]

## 1. Coroners Act 2010 — the duty triggered by the death

Where a person dies while in any hospital or medical clinic for medical treatment or care, the **person in charge of the hospital** must preserve all medical records, healthcare records and any other document pertaining to the medical treatment or care of the deceased that are in the hospital's possession, for the period prescribed by regulations. [CITE:1]

The same preservation duty applies to a person who dies while in official custody, so the provision covers hospitals, medical clinics and places of custody. [CITE:1]

Failure to comply without reasonable excuse is an offence, punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding $10,000, imprisonment not exceeding 12 months, or both, and the accused bears the burden of proving the reasonable excuse. [CITE:1]

The length of the preservation period is not stated in the provisions supplied: section 8 requires preservation "for such period as may be prescribed", so the exact duration must be found in the regulations made under the Coroners Act 2010, which are not among the sources provided and can be checked on Singapore Statutes Online. [CITE:1]

## 2. Healthcare Services Act 2020 — record-keeping by licensees

A licensee must keep and maintain records, for the prescribed period and in the prescribed manner, where the records are relevant to the monitoring or evaluation of any aspect of a licensable healthcare service or its provision. [CITE:2]

The regulated services include acute hospital service, community hospital service, ambulatory surgical centre service, clinical laboratory service, emergency ambulance service, outpatient medical service, nursing home service and other listed services. [CITE:15]

A licensee must also implement prescribed safeguards protecting those records and the computer systems used to hold them against accidental or unlawful loss, modification or destruction, and against unauthorised access, disclosure, copying, use or modification; must monitor and periodically evaluate those safeguards; and must ensure that staff who access or handle the records know the safeguards and their own role in maintaining the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the records. [CITE:2]

A licensee must take reasonable care when disposing of or destroying records so as to prevent unauthorised access to, or unauthorised disclosure or reproduction of, the record or the information in it, and must not record matters inaccurately or incompletely, or leave records out of date, in purported compliance with the record-keeping duty. [CITE:2]

Contravention of section 27 is an offence, punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding $20,000, imprisonment not exceeding 12 months, or both. [CITE:2]

The Minister may make regulations prescribing, among other things, the records of patients, customers and staff that licensees must keep and maintain, and the safeguards licensees must implement to protect those records and computer systems against loss, modification, destruction and unauthorised access, disclosure, copying, use or modification. [CITE:9] [CITE:5]

## 3. What happens to the records after the death

Preservation does not insulate the records from lawful use. When a Coroner or the Public Prosecutor receives information about a death, that officer may direct a forensic pathologist to investigate the cause and circumstances of the death and direct that copies of all medical records, healthcare records and other relevant documents be furnished by the person in charge of the hospital, medical clinic or place of custody, or any other person in possession of them. [CITE:3]

The forensic pathologist may require a medical practitioner or healthcare practitioner to furnish a detailed report on the care rendered before death, the relevant medical or healthcare records, and any other information, substance or thing in that practitioner's possession considered necessary for the investigation; it is an offence, punishable by a fine up to $10,000 or imprisonment up to 12 months or both, to fail to provide these without reasonable excuse, to provide information known or believed to be false or incomplete, or to tamper with or destroy the records. [CITE:8]

Where a body has remained unclaimed from an approved hospital or an institution maintained on public funds for more than 24 hours after death, the Director-General may authorise in writing a post-mortem examination to establish or confirm the cause of death or to investigate the existence or nature of abnormal conditions. [CITE:14]

The Director-General or an authorised officer may, at any time and without notice or warrant, enter, inspect and search premises used to provide a healthcare service or to store information relating to it, in order to investigate offences, licence compliance, or whether the licensee's practices and procedures comply with the Act or an applicable code of practice, and may inspect and copy any medical record of individuals treated there or provided a licensable healthcare service even without prior consent. [CITE:7]

However, those officials are themselves restricted: they must not disclose medical information obtained in the course of their functions except in the specified statutory circumstances, or with the consent of the individual or, for a deceased person, their "representative", which includes the executor, administrator or next-of-kin. [CITE:12] [CITE:6]

## 4. Why records matter beyond the coronial process

In the Court of Appeal decision in Noor Azlin binte Abdul Rahman v Changi General Hospital, the court found that because there was no record of the senior doctor who had reviewed the radiological reports and decided not to recall the patient, it was more likely than not that the hospital's procedure had not been adhered to and that the hospital had failed to ensure proper follow-up. [CITE:16] The court also held that a review system which did not require reviewing doctors to record their decisions and the reasons for not following the radiologist's recommendation fell below the standard of care owed by the hospital and lacked accountability. [CITE:18]

In short, the hospital must preserve the deceased's medical records under the Coroners Act, and as a licensee it must also comply with the Healthcare Services Act record-keeping rules, with criminal penalties attaching to an unjustified failure to preserve them. [CITE:1] [CITE:2]

**As at 2026-11-06, yes — in principle your son is eligible for probation despite the mandatory minimum sentence, but probation remains a matter of the sentencing court's discretion rather than an entitlement.** [CITE:1]

## 1. The statutory route that applies

Under section 5(1) of the Probation of Offenders Act 1951, a court may, instead of sentencing a person convicted of an offence whose sentence is not fixed by law, make a probation order if it considers it expedient having regard to the circumstances, including the nature of the offence and the character of the offender. [CITE:1]

That subsection contains an express proviso for offences carrying a specified minimum sentence, or a mandatory minimum sentence, of imprisonment, fine or caning: in those cases the court may still make a probation order if the person (a) had attained 16 years but not 21 years of age at the time of conviction, and (b) has not previously been convicted of any such offence. [CITE:1] The proviso also provides that the deeming provision in section 11(1) is to be disregarded when checking any previous conviction of that kind. [CITE:1] A probation order may run for a period of not less than 6 months and not more than 3 years. [CITE:1]

## 2. Application to your son

A mandatory minimum sentence is not the same as an offence whose sentence is "fixed by law"; the proviso specifically contemplates offences with specified or mandatory minimum sentences and keeps probation available for them in the stated circumstances. [CITE:1]

On the facts given, your son satisfies both conditions of the proviso: at 19 he had attained 16 but not 21 at the time of conviction, and this is his first conviction for an offence of that kind. [CITE:1] The mandatory minimum sentence therefore does not, by itself, prevent a probation order. [CITE:1]

Whether the offence really carries a prescribed specified or mandatory minimum sentence depends on the specific written law under which he was convicted, which the sources provided do not identify. [CITE:14] The First Schedule to the Prisons Act 1933, for example, lists a range of offences (including certain offences under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1973 and the Children and Young Persons Act 1993) with one-year minimum sentences, in the context of the mandatory aftercare scheme, although the extract supplied is partial. [CITE:14]

## 3. The court's discretion and the safeguards

Probation is still conditional on the court forming the view that it is expedient in the circumstances, including the nature of the offence and your son's character; the proviso removes the sentencing barrier but not the discretion. [CITE:1]

Before making the order, the court must explain to him in ordinary language what the order means, including any additional requirements, and that if he fails to comply or commits another offence he will be liable to be sentenced for the original offence; because he is not less than 14 years of age, he must also express his willingness to comply before the order can be made. [CITE:8] A probation order may also carry requirements relating to residence, and unpaid community service under supervision. [CITE:1]

## 4. If the minimum is expressed as a presumptive minimum

If the statute expresses the minimum as "imprisonment for a presumptive minimum term of not less than", section 303A(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 provides that, unless the context requires otherwise, a reference in any written law to a mandatory minimum sentence of imprisonment includes a reference to such a presumptive minimum, so the probation proviso is engaged on the same footing. [CITE:9]

Under section 303A, the court must impose a sentence equal to or greater than the presumptive minimum unless exceptional circumstances would make it unjust to do so for a first-time offender, in which case a sentence of the same type but shorter may be imposed; the statutory explanation states that a guilty plea, first-time offender status and previous good character are not by themselves sufficient to constitute exceptional circumstances. [CITE:9]

Note that "first-time offender" in section 303A is a wider test than having no previous mandatory-minimum conviction: it excludes anyone previously sentenced to imprisonment for any offence (other than imprisonment in default of a fine), to reformative training, corrective training or preventive detention, previously detained or subject to police supervision under the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act 1955, or previously admitted to an approved institution or approved centre. [CITE:9] The sources provided do not state how section 303A operates when the sentencing court instead makes a probation order under the Probation of Offenders Act, so that interaction would need to be checked against the current statutory text on Singapore Statutes Online or with a lawyer. [CITE:1][CITE:9]

## 5. The Youth Court route

Because he is 19, the Youth Court route may also be open: where a Youth Court is satisfied that an offence has been proved, it may make a probation order requiring supervision by a probation officer or volunteer probation officer for not less than 6 months and not more than 3 years. [CITE:10] Section 323 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 also allows a court that convicts a juvenile of an offence punishable by fine or imprisonment to deal with the juvenile under the Children and Young Persons Act 1993 instead of fining or sentencing. [CITE:17] The definitions of "child", "young person" and "juvenile", and the Youth Court's age jurisdiction, are not reproduced in the sources provided, so whether your son falls within them cannot be confirmed from these materials. [CITE:10][CITE:17]

## 6. What a probation order would mean for him

Probation is not without consequences. If it appears to a magistrate during the probation period that the probationer has failed to comply with any requirement, the Magistrate's Court may impose a fine not exceeding $1,000, order detention in prison for a period not exceeding 14 days, or, where the order was made by the General Division of the High Court or a District Court, commit the probationer to custody or release him on bail to be brought before the court that made the order. [CITE:7] If he is convicted of an offence committed during the probation period and dealt with for it, the court which made the probation order may then deal with him in respect of the original offence, and the extract of section 9(5) provided ends at that point. [CITE:6]

On the conviction itself, section 11(1) provides that a conviction for an offence for which probation is ordered is deemed not to be a conviction for any purpose other than the proceedings in which the order is made and any subsequent proceedings under the Act; because he was 16 or older at conviction, that protection ceases if he is subsequently sentenced under the Act for that same offence. [CITE:3] Section 11(2) additionally disregards the conviction for the purposes of any written law imposing a disqualification or disability on convicted persons. [CITE:3] Section 41 of the Children and Young Persons Act 1993 provides that a conviction or finding of guilt of a child or young person is disregarded for the purposes of any Act imposing a disqualification or disability. [CITE:19]

## 7. A related distinction

The general community-order regime in Part 17 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 is separately barred for offences for which a specified minimum sentence of imprisonment or caning, or a mandatory minimum sentence of imprisonment, fine or caning, is prescribed, subject to limited exceptions for mandatory treatment orders and community work orders. [CITE:11] A probation order under the Probation of Offenders Act 1951 is a separate order and is not excluded by that bar. [CITE:1]

The statutory extracts supplied are the 2020 Edition of the Probation of Offenders Act 1951 and consolidated versions of the other Acts, so the current text on Singapore Statutes Online should be checked for any later amendment. [CITE:1][CITE:9][CITE:10]

- **Personal-liability gateway:** Proceedings cannot be brought against the Government unless damages proceedings would have lain personally against the officer. Any written law limiting an officer’s liability also applies to proceedings against the Government. [CITE:2]
- **Government officers:** The officer must satisfy the statutory employment-and-payment requirements, and liability is excluded for acts connected with specified judicial responsibilities. [CITE:2]

As at 2026-11-06, **yes, potentially**: section 4(3) of the Community Disputes Resolution Act expressly allows a qualifying neighbour to bring civil proceedings in a court against a respondent for wrongful conduct causing unreasonable interference with the neighbour’s enjoyment or use of their place of residence. [CITE:2]

### When you can bring proceedings

- Under section 4(4), a “neighbour” is someone who lawfully resides in the same building as the respondent or within 100 metres of the respondent’s place of residence, but excludes someone occupying the **same place of residence** as the respondent. The illustrations state that people living in different rooms of the same apartment occupy the same place of residence and are therefore not neighbours under this section. [CITE:2]
- The claim must concern an act or omission that directly or indirectly causes **unreasonable interference** with your enjoyment or use of your place of residence. The section expressly identifies excessive noise as a possible form of interference. [CITE:2]
- Nightly noise is not automatically actionable merely because it occurs every night; the central question is whether the interference was unreasonable in the circumstances. The supplied case law also describes nuisance as requiring a factual balancing of conflicting interests, and the type of premises and the way they are used can affect that assessment. [CITE:9][CITE:13]
- The supplied section contains no fixed decibel threshold. [CITE:2]

### What the court must consider

Under section 5(1), the court may make an order if it is satisfied **on the balance of probabilities** that the section 4 claim has been made out and that it is **just and equitable** to do so. [CITE:1]

In deciding whether an order is just and equitable, the court must consider the order’s impact on the respondent, anyone residing in the same place of residence, and anyone else who can reasonably be expected to be affected. [CITE:1]

The court must also consider the ordinary instances of daily living that can reasonably be expected to be tolerated by reasonable persons living in Singapore, which is directly relevant to recurring noise affecting use of a home. [CITE:1]

The court may consider any other matters it considers appropriate. [CITE:1]

Case law explains that nuisance liability can exist independently of negligence, so proving that the respondent took all reasonable care is not, by itself, a defence once nuisance is proved. [CITE:10]

### Orders the court may make

If the statutory requirements are satisfied, the court may order damages, an injunction, specific performance, an apology, any other order authorised under the Act, and necessary ancillary orders. [CITE:1]

A consent order, or an order made in a party’s absence under the prescribed Rules of Court, has the same force and effect as an order made after a hearing. [CITE:1]

### Mediation

The Act also permits an authorised community relations officer and specified other authorities to direct the individuals involved in a neighbour dispute, and a relevant landlord, to a Community Mediation Centre or another prescribed mediation entity, with or without the affected persons’ consent. [CITE:12]

Accordingly, court proceedings are legally available where the noise amounts to unreasonable interference and the neighbour meets the statutory definition, but the supplied law does not permit a definitive prediction from nightly noise alone because reasonableness, impact, and the circumstances of the properties remain fact-dependent. [CITE:2][CITE:9][CITE:13]

**As at 2026-11-06, the maximum number of non-constituency Members of Parliament is 12.** [CITE:1]

**Constitutional ceiling.** Article 39(1)(b) of the Constitution provides for "such other Members, not exceeding 12 in number, who shall be known as non-constituency Members", as the Legislature may provide by law relating to Parliamentary elections, to ensure representation in Parliament of a minimum number of Members from a political party or parties not forming the Government. [CITE:1]

**How the number is worked out in practice.** Under section 52(1) of the Parliamentary Elections Act 1954, the number of non-constituency Members declared elected at a general election is the whole number (ignoring any fraction) ascertained under the formula 12 − B, where B is the total number of Opposition Members elected to Parliament. [CITE:2] The formula therefore produces a maximum of 12 and a smaller number where Opposition Members have already been elected to constituency seats. [CITE:2]

**Candidates and vacancies.** Non-constituency Members are selected from among the candidates of parties other than the party or parties that will form the Government, ranked by the percentage of votes they polled, with a candidate required to have polled at least 15% of the valid votes in the electoral division contested. [CITE:2] If a non-constituency Member fails to take the Oath of Allegiance, Parliament may by resolution declare the seat vacant, in which case the next succeeding candidate in that order who is eligible and has polled at least 15% is deemed elected. [CITE:8]

**Not to be confused with nominated Members.** Nominated Members of Parliament, appointed by the President on nomination of the Special Select Committee, are a separate category capped at 9. [CITE:1] [CITE:12]

**As at 2026-11-06, Singapore law provides a statutory route for asking the court to stay (put on hold) court proceedings, but only so far as those proceedings relate to a matter covered by the arbitration agreement, and only if you apply within a defined window.**

## 1. Who can apply, and when

Any party to the arbitration agreement may apply to the court to stay the proceedings so far as they relate to the matter that is the subject of the agreement [CITE:1] [CITE:2].

The application must be made **after** a notice of intention to contest or not contest has been filed and served, and **before** you deliver any pleading (other than a pleading asserting that the court does not have jurisdiction) or take any other step in the proceedings [CITE:1] [CITE:2].

A "party" includes any person claiming through or under a party [CITE:1] [CITE:2]. Under the International Arbitration Act 1994, "court" means the General Division of the High Court, the District Court, the Magistrate's Court or any other court in which the proceedings are instituted [CITE:2].

## 2. What the court must do

**Domestic arbitration — Arbitration Act 2001, section 6(2):** the court **may** stay the proceedings if it is satisfied that (a) there is no sufficient reason why the matter should not be referred in accordance with the arbitration agreement, and (b) the applicant was, at the time the proceedings were commenced, and still remains, ready and willing to do all things necessary for the proper conduct of the arbitration; the court may impose any terms it thinks fit [CITE:1].

**International commercial arbitration — International Arbitration Act 1994, section 6(2):** the court **is to** make an order staying the proceedings, on such terms or conditions as it thinks fit, unless it is satisfied that the arbitration agreement is null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed [CITE:2]. This section applies despite Article 8 of the Model Law [CITE:2]. So the court's role is narrower here than under the domestic provision [CITE:1] [CITE:2].

## 3. Scope of the stay

The stay extends only to the proceedings **in so far as they relate to** the arbitrated matter; a claim falling outside the arbitration clause is not stayed by the order [CITE:1] [CITE:2].

Whether a court proceeding is "in respect of a matter which is the subject of the agreement" can therefore be a live question. In *Spandeck Engineering (S) Pte Ltd v Defence Science & Technology Agency* [2006] SGHC 229, a General Division decision at first instance and therefore persuasive rather than binding on higher courts, the defendant did not use the contract's arbitration clause to seek a stay, apparently because the claim was framed in tort rather than in contract, and the court observed that arbitration was an available contractual remedy and that the plaintiff should look to the employer for redress under the contract [CITE:12].

## 4. Conditions the court may impose and security

Under section 6(3) of both Acts, when making a stay order the court may make interim or supplementary orders it thinks fit for the purpose of preserving the rights of the parties in relation to property that is, or forms part of, the subject of the dispute [CITE:1] [CITE:2].

Under section 7 of the Arbitration Act 2001 and section 7 of the International Arbitration Act 1994, if property has been arrested or bail or other security was given in the proceedings, the court may order that the arrested property be retained as security for the satisfaction of any award made in the arbitration, or make the stay conditional on the provision of equivalent security; the same law and practice apply to retained property as in the court proceedings, subject to the Rules of Court and any necessary modification [CITE:3] [CITE:5].

## 5. If proceedings stall after a stay

Where no party has taken any further step in the proceedings for a period of at least two years after a stay order was made, the court may, on its own motion, discontinue the proceedings, without prejudice to the right of any party to apply for reinstatement [CITE:1] [CITE:2].

## 6. Related provisions that are distinct from a stay

- If a court grants interpleader relief and an issue between claimants falls within their arbitration agreement, the court may direct that the issue be determined in accordance with the agreement [CITE:8].
- The court has powers in support of arbitral proceedings, including securing the amount in dispute, preventing dissipation of assets, and granting interim injunctions or other interim measures [CITE:17]; for international arbitrations, the General Division of the High Court has court-ordered interim measure powers even where the place of arbitration is outside Singapore [CITE:20].

- Where the court sets aside an award, it may also order that a provision making the award a condition precedent to bringing legal proceedings is of no effect as regards the subject matter of the award [CITE:14].
- Other statutes provide separate stay routes: section 8 of the Mediation Act 2017 for proceedings relating to a matter under a mediation agreement [CITE:9], and section 13 of the Lease Agreements for Retail Premises Act 2023 for proceedings relating to a complaint of non-compliance under that Act [CITE:6].

The sources supplied do not include the wording of your arbitration clause, any authority on how the domestic section 6(2) threshold is applied in practice, or any provision stating what follows if a stay application is refused [CITE:1] [CITE:2]. As at 2026-11-06, yes — under Singapore's Protection from Scams Act 2025, a "specified officer" can issue a restriction order that stops a bank from letting a scam victim transfer or withdraw money, and from granting a credit facility, once the statutory conditions are met. [CITE:1][CITE:2] The consolidated text supplied here is the version in force from 1 July 2025, so the Singapore Statutes Online should be checked for any later amendments. [CITE:1][CITE:2]

## Who can be stopped, and what the order does

The Act applies to a "scam victim", defined as an individual against whom a scam offence is committed or intended to be committed, with "scam offence" meaning any offence specified in the Schedule to the Act. [CITE:9]

A restriction order is an order issued by a specified officer to one or more banks that directs the bank not to allow any transfer or withdrawal of money from any account of the scam victim maintained with that bank, and not to grant or allow a drawdown of any credit facility to the scam victim, and it specifies when the direction takes effect. [CITE:1] A "bank account" includes an account where money is held in the names of two or more persons, at least one of whom is the scam victim, so a joint account can be caught. [CITE:9] "Credit facility" covers advances, loans or other facilities granted by a bank to an individual customer that give access to funds or financial guarantees, and any other liability incurred by a bank on behalf of an individual customer. [CITE:9]

## When an order may be issued

A specified officer may, on receipt of any information, issue a restriction order where the officer has reason to believe the scam victim will instruct a bank to transfer money to a scammer (directly or through an intermediary), withdraw money intending to give it to a scammer, or apply for or draw down a credit facility with the intention of benefiting a scammer. [CITE:2] "Scammer" means a person whom the officer has reason to believe has committed, participated in, facilitated, or taken preparatory steps toward a scam offence against the victim, and who has interacted with the victim through remote communication for that purpose. [CITE:2][CITE:9]

The order must also be necessary for the victim's protection, having regard to the time required by any specified officer, relative of the victim or other persons (including non-profit and non-governmental organisations) to implement measures to reduce the risk of the victim becoming, or continuing to be, a victim of a scam offence, and to all other relevant circumstances. [CITE:2] "Relative" is defined to include the victim's spouse, siblings and stepsiblings, children (including adopted children), stepchildren, grandchildren and step-grandchildren, nephews and nieces with their step equivalents; children of the victim are therefore within the defined category. [CITE:2]

Age alone is not a listed criterion in the material provided; the relevant questions are the officer's belief about the victim's intended dealings and the necessity of the order for protection. [CITE:2]

## Duration, cancellation, variation and extension

A restriction order is in force for 30 days or any shorter period specified in the order. [CITE:3] A specified officer may cancel it at any time, and cancellation does not affect the operation of the order or anything done or omitted in compliance with it before cancellation. [CITE:3] On the application of the scam victim or a joint account holder, a specified officer may vary the order to permit the bank to allow a transfer or withdrawal on the applicant's instruction, subject to any limit or terms the officer specifies. [CITE:3] The officer may extend the order for a period of up to 30 days at a time if more time is required to reduce the risk of the victim becoming or continuing to be a scam victim, and the order must not be extended more than five times. [CITE:3]

## Position of the bank

A bank that contravenes a restriction order without reasonable excuse commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine of up to $3,000, and a specified officer may compound the offence by collecting up to $1,500. [CITE:4] No criminal or civil liability is incurred by a bank, or by its officers, employees or agents, for anything done or omitted with reasonable care and in good faith in complying with a restriction order. [CITE:7]

## Appeals

A scam victim, and any joint account holder of the victim's account with a bank subject to the order, may appeal to the Commissioner against a specified officer's decision about a restriction order. [CITE:11] The appeal must be in the prescribed form, specify the grounds, include the prescribed documents or information, and be made within the prescribed period after receipt of the notification of the decision. [CITE:11] The Commissioner may reject an appeal that fails to comply with those requirements, may consider documents or information other than those submitted, and may decide the appeal on documentary evidence without holding a hearing. [CITE:11] The Commissioner may reject the appeal and confirm the decision, or allow it and revoke, substitute or vary the decision, and the decision on appeal is final. [CITE:11] An appeal does not suspend the decision: the decision must still be complied with until the appeal is determined, unless the Commissioner directs otherwise. [CITE:11]

## Other freezing powers in the supplied material

The other account-freezing powers provided in these sources address different situations and do not cover scam victims: freezing of a mutual benefit organisation's funds after a notice from the Registrar under the Mutual Benefit Organisations Act; [CITE:5] freezing for ransom payments under the Hostage-Taking Act and the Kidnapping Act; [CITE:6][CITE:8] freezing of a co-operative society's funds under the Co-operative Societies Act; [CITE:16] and court orders in regulatory investigations under the Financial Advisers Act. [CITE:12] The remaining Banking Act and Moneylenders Act provisions supplied concern bank solvency control, director disqualification, business transfers, deposit-taking and inspection of moneylending premises rather than protection of scam victims. [CITE:19][CITE:10][CITE:13][CITE:14][CITE:17][CITE:15][CITE:18]

One limitation in the material supplied: the excerpt of the interpretation section ends part-way through the definition of "specified officer", so the precise list of officers empowered to issue orders is not shown here. [CITE:9] The full current definition can be found in the Protection from Scams Act 2025 on Singapore Statutes Online. [CITE:9]

answer:
As at 2026-11-06, publishing a person's home address and phone number online in order to frighten them can engage several offences in Singapore, most directly the Protection from Harassment Act 2014, and, if a threat was made, the Penal Code [CITE:3][CITE:4][CITE:5][CITE:8][CITE:9]. The extracts supplied are the consolidated versions stated to be in force from 15 October 2024 (Protection from Harassment Act), 30 May 2025 (Penal Code), 5 December 2025 (Personal Data Protection Act), 8 December 2025 (Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act), 1 September 2025 (Online Criminal Harms Act) and 5 December 2025 (Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act), with the source extracts themselves directing that Singapore Statutes Online be checked for the latest version [CITE:1][CITE:3][CITE:4][CITE:6][CITE:7][CITE:9][CITE:15][CITE:20].

## The main provisions that fit your description

**Intentionally causing harassment, alarm or distress — section 3.** An individual or entity must not, with intent to cause harassment, alarm or distress to a target person, use threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour, make a threatening, abusive or insulting communication, or publish any identity information of the target person or a related person, where the result is that the target or any other person suffers harassment, alarm or distress [CITE:9]. On your account, the post of your home address and phone number was made to scare you and produced that result, which maps onto the intent-and-result elements of section 3 [CITE:9]. Punishment on conviction is a fine not exceeding $5,000, imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months, or both [CITE:9]. The defendant may prove as a defence that the conduct was reasonable [CITE:9].

**Fear, provocation or facilitation of violence — section 5.** An individual or entity must not publish any identity information of another person with intent to cause that person to believe unlawful violence will be used against them or another person, or to facilitate the use of unlawful violence against them or another person; the offence also applies where the accused knew, or had reasonable cause to believe, that this was likely [CITE:5]. A published home address is precisely the information that makes it possible to find and confront a person, and this provision expressly reaches facilitation of violence [CITE:5]. Punishment on conviction is a fine not exceeding $5,000, imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months, or both [CITE:5]. The defences are that the accused had no reason to believe the words, behaviour or communication would be perceived by the victim, or that the conduct was reasonable [CITE:5]. The supplied extracts do not set out the Act's definition of "identity information", so the exact statutory scope of that term cannot be confirmed from these sources alone [CITE:5][CITE:9].

**Harassment, alarm or distress without proof of intent — section 4.** It is an offence to use threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour, or make a threatening, abusive or insulting communication, which is heard, seen or otherwise perceived by any person and is likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress [CITE:8]. Section 4 therefore turns on both the content of the post and its likely effect, so it applies where the posting also contained threatening or abusive material [CITE:8]. Punishment on conviction is a fine not exceeding $5,000 [CITE:8]. The defences are that the accused had no reason to believe the material would be perceived by the victim, or that the conduct was reasonable [CITE:8].

**Unlawful stalking — section 7.** An individual or entity must not unlawfully stalk another person, which requires a course of conduct involving acts or omissions associated with stalking, causing harassment, alarm or distress, and carried out with intent to cause that result or with knowledge or reason to know it is likely [CITE:16]. Examples of acts associated with stalking include making communications by any means relating to the victim, giving or sending material to the victim or leaving it where the victim will find it, and keeping the victim under surveillance [CITE:16]. A single post is one act, so section 7 becomes relevant where there is a wider course of conduct, such as repeated postings or subsequent unwanted contact [CITE:16].

**Criminal intimidation — section 503 of the Penal Code.** A person commits criminal intimidation by threatening another with injury to their person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of anyone in whom the threatened person is interested, with intent to cause alarm or to make the person do, or omit, an act they are not legally bound or entitled to do, as the means of avoiding execution of the threat [CITE:4]. The statutory illustration is of a person threatening to burn another's house to make him desist from a civil suit [CITE:4]. This section therefore depends on a threat meeting those elements being made, rather than on the disclosure of personal details alone [CITE:4].

## Civil orders and extra-territorial reach

**Protection orders — section 12.** Where the court is satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the contravention involves an offending communication, and that the respondent or a third party has published or is likely to publish the offending communication through an internet intermediary service provided by an internet intermediary, the court may, if it is just and equitable in the circumstances, order that intermediary to disable access in Singapore by end-users to the offending communication, or, for a prescribed internet intermediary, to any identical copy [CITE:11]. A protection order may also include requirements necessary or incidental to carrying it into effect, may be subject to specified exceptions or conditions, and ceases to have effect after the period specified by the court, subject to the court's power to vary, suspend, cancel or extend it [CITE:11]. Section 17(1) confirms that the court has jurisdiction to make orders under section 12 or 13, although the text of section 13 is not among the supplied sources [CITE:3].

**Jurisdiction where the poster is outside Singapore — section 17.** For a contravention of section 3 where the accused was outside Singapore when the words, behaviour, communication or publication occurred, the court has jurisdiction if the victim was in Singapore when the contravention caused harassment, alarm or distress, and the accused knew or had reason to believe the victim would be in Singapore [CITE:3]. Equivalent rules apply to contraventions of sections 4, 5 and 6 where the accused was outside Singapore [CITE:3].

## Other regimes that do not directly cover the posting

**Unsolicited messages to the published number.** The Do Not Call provisions of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 address sending messages rather than publishing personal details: section 43 prohibits sending a specified message addressed to a Singapore telephone number unless the sender has valid confirmation that the number is not listed in the relevant register, subject to an exception where the subscriber or user gave clear and unambiguous consent that is evidenced in writing or other form accessible for subsequent reference [CITE:17]. Section 44 requires such a message to include clear and accurate information identifying the individual or organisation that sent or authorised it, clear and accurate information on how the recipient can readily contact it, any prescribed information, and information that is reasonably likely to be valid for at least 30 days after the message is sent [CITE:14]. Section 48B prohibits sending an applicable message to an applicable telephone number, which is a number generated or obtained through a dictionary attack or through address-harvesting software, subject to a good-faith employee exception [CITE:1][CITE:6]. These provisions are relevant to any unsolicited calls or messages sent to numbers harvested from the posting [CITE:1][CITE:6][CITE:14][CITE:17].

**Declaration and prohibition mechanisms.** A declared online location under the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act 2019 requires three or more different statements that are the subject of active Part 3 or Part 4 Directions communicated in Singapore on that online location [CITE:2]. ## The rule

Section 12(1) applies where an exclusive choice of court agreement does not designate any Singapore court as the chosen court: despite any other written law or rule of law, a Singapore court must stay or dismiss any case or proceeding to which the agreement applies [CITE:1].

## The exceptions

The stay or dismissal is not required if the Singapore court determines that any one of the following applies [CITE:1]:

- **(a) Nullity in the chosen court’s State:** the agreement is null and void under the law of the State of the chosen court [CITE:1].
- **(b) Lack of capacity:** a party to the agreement lacked capacity under the law of Singapore to enter into or conclude it [CITE:1].
- **(c) Manifest injustice or public policy:** giving effect to the agreement would lead to a manifest injustice, or would be manifestly contrary to the public policy of Singapore [CITE:1].
- **(d) Exceptional inability to perform:** the agreement cannot reasonably be performed for exceptional reasons beyond the control of the parties to it [CITE:1].
- **(e) Chosen court declines to hear the case:** the chosen court has decided not to hear the case or proceeding [CITE:1].

## Other grounds for staying or dismissing are preserved

Section 12(1) does not affect the ability of a Singapore court to stay or dismiss the case or proceeding on other grounds [CITE:1].

## When this rule applies

- Section 8 applies the Act in every international case where there is an exclusive choice of court agreement concluded in a civil or commercial matter, subject to sections 9, 10 and 22 [CITE:11].
- An exclusive choice of court agreement is an agreement, in writing or recorded by a communication usable for subsequent reference, that designates the courts (or specific courts) of one Contracting State to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of any other court for disputes arising or arising in connection with a particular legal relationship [CITE:7]; an agreement meeting the stated requirements is deemed exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise [CITE:7].
- A “chosen court” means a court of a Contracting State designated in an exclusive choice of court agreement, and a “Contracting State” means a State party to the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements of 30 June 2005 (with the extended meaning for certain regional economic integration organisations and their member States) [CITE:15].
- For Part 2, a case is international unless the parties reside in the same Contracting State and the relationship of the parties and all other relevant elements of the dispute (other than the location of the chosen court) are connected only with that Contracting State [CITE:12].
- The Act does not apply where a party is an individual acting primarily as a consumer, or where the agreement relates to a contract of employment or a collective agreement [CITE:10]; nor does it apply to the listed excluded matters, such as family law, succession, insolvency, carriage of passengers and goods, competition law, and non-contractual property damage claims [CITE:10]; nor to arbitration or arbitration-related proceedings [CITE:10].
- The Act does not apply to interim measures of protection, and nothing prevents a party from applying to a Singapore court for, or the court from granting, an interim measure of protection in a case involving an exclusive choice of court agreement [CITE:9].
- The Act does not apply to an exclusive choice of court agreement designating a Singapore court that was concluded before 1 October 2016; to an agreement designating a court of another Contracting State that was concluded before the Convention entered into force in that Contracting State; or to any case instituted in a Singapore court before 1 October 2016 or any application made in such a case [CITE:4].

**As at 2026-11-06,** under the Civil Law Act 1909 (Singapore) [CITE:6], damages for bereavement are available where death is caused by a wrongful act, neglect or default that would have supported an action by the injured person had the death not ensued [CITE:2]. The claim may be included in an action under section 20 [CITE:1].

## Who may benefit, in priority order

Section 21(2) sets out a ranked list, and the claim is available only for the benefit of persons who **survive the deceased** [CITE:1]. For an unmarried deceased with no children:

1. **Spouse — none.** Paragraph (a) refers to the wife or husband of the deceased, and there is no spouse here [CITE:1].
2. **Children — none.** Paragraph (b) applies only where there is no person who can claim under paragraph (a) or (b), and the deceased had no children [CITE:1].
3. **Parents.** Because no person can claim under (a) or (b), the **parents of the deceased** may benefit; if the deceased was illegitimate, **only the mother** may benefit in this category [CITE:1]. Paragraph (c) refers to the parents without any requirement that they were financially dependent on the deceased [CITE:1].
4. **Minor treated as a child of the family.** If no person can claim under (a), (b) or (c) **and the deceased was a minor at the date of death**, any person who, during any marriage to which that person was a party, treated the deceased as a child of the family in relation to that marriage may benefit [CITE:1].
5. **Brothers and sisters.** Only if **no other person** can claim under subsection (2) may a brother or sister of the deceased benefit [CITE:1].

Although section 20(8) defines "dependant" to include a former wife, the categories of people who may benefit specifically from **bereavement** damages are those listed in section 21(2), which refers to the deceased's wife or husband [CITE:2][CITE:1].

## Bringing the claim

- The action must be brought by and in the name of the deceased's **executor or administrator** [CITE:2].
- If there is no executor or administrator, or no action is brought within **six months after the death**, the action may be brought by and in the name of all or any of the persons for whose benefit the executor or administrator could have brought it [CITE:2].
- Not more than one action may lie for the same subject matter of complaint, and the action must be brought within **three years after the death** [CITE:2].
- The right of a beneficiary to claim does not survive for the benefit of that person's estate [CITE:1].

## Amount and related awards

- The sum awarded as damages for bereavement is **$15,000** under section 21(4), subject to the Minister's power under section 21(6) to substitute another sum by order published in the Gazette [CITE:1]. A 2008 Court of Appeal judgment described the section 21(4) award as $10,000 [CITE:7]; on the materials provided, the $15,000 figure in the current consolidated statutory text prevails over the figure stated in that earlier judgment [CITE:1][CITE:7].
- Where two or more persons benefit, the sum is divided equally between them, subject to any deduction for costs not recovered from the defendant [CITE:1]; unrecovered costs are also deducted before damages are divided among dependants [CITE:4].
- Damages are assessed so as to be proportionate to the losses resulting from the death to the dependants, and damages for funeral expenses may also be awarded [CITE:4].
- Where the death was caused by an offence, the criminal court may order the offender to pay compensation to a dependant for bereavement damages, and for funeral expenses where incurred, whether or not any section 20 action is brought [CITE:5].
